newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Report shows bow visor cause of Estonia ferry - agency.
newsitem.headline: Report shows bow visor cause of Estonia ferry - agency.

text.p: The much-delayed official report into the sinking of the Estonia car ferry in 1994 will conclude that human error was not the main cause, the Estonian chairman of a three-nation commission into the accident was quoted on Saturday as saying.

Uno Laur told the Swedish news agency TT in an interview that the massive report into the accident, in which 852 people perished, would confirm a preliminary report's findings that poor design of the ferry's bow visor was at fault.
The visor, which lifts up and down to allow cars on and off, was ripped off the ship during a storm in the Baltic Sea as the ferry sailed from Tallinn to Stockholm.
Water flooded onto the ship's cavernous car deck, destabilising the vessel and sending it to the seabed. Only around 100 people survived the disaster. 500 of the dead were Swedes.
Laur said the mainly Estonian crew did not make any serious mistakes but were a few minutes slow in sounding emergency alarms.
The official report has been delayed several times and the commission -- made up of Estonian, Swedish and Finnish maritime officials -- has been riven by disputes.
The construction of the bow visor was deficient, the locks which attached it to the ship were too small and had not been repaired or changed since the ship left the shipyard in 1980, Laur said.
Laur said the report would also question why classification society Bureau Veritas did not report that Estonia's sister ship Diana II in 1993 had a serious incident with its ramp.
Laur was quoted as saying: "It is not our business to criticise, we should only give the facts."
He said the crew may have been slow in sending a Mayday signal. "But we still do not know what happened on the bridge," he said.

Although Estonian ship captain Arvo Andresen did not handle the Mayday signal and the contact with nearby ships, the commission has found that he was on the bridge at seven minutes past one a.m., about 40 minutes before Estonia sank, Laur said.
"My personal view is that something very serious happened to the captain, an accident of some kind - he might have fallen on the bridge," Laur said.
